meta.description: Verified. Audrey Hepburn said it in a New York Times interview published 22 April 1991 — printed wording begins "I myself was born…".
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I was born with an enormous need for affection, and a terrible need to give it'?
meta.ogDescription: Hepburn really did say it — to The New York Times, 22 April 1991. The printed line keeps one word the internet drops: "myself".

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: She said it to Alan Riding of The New York Times in an interview at her home in Switzerland, printed on 22 April 1991 — the day the Film Society of Lincoln Center honoured her career at Avery Fisher Hall. The line survives almost intact in circulation: the paper printed “I myself was born with an enormous need for affection and a terrible need to give it,” and the popular version simply drops the word “myself.”

source.excerpt: “I myself was born with an enormous need for affection and a terrible need to give it,” she went on. “That’s what I’d like to think maybe has been the appeal.”
trail: Alan Riding interviewed Hepburn in Switzerland for a piece published on 22 April 1991 ↗, the day the Film Society of Lincoln Center honoured her at Avery Fisher Hall.

Pressed on why audiences opened up to her, she answered that for her it always had to do with “some kind of affection, love, a warmth” — and then gave the line, printed as direct speech in Section C, Page 13 ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced quotes and cites that same 1991 Times interview — not its Misattributed section.
Aggregator copies such as this Goodreads entry ↗ print the trimmed wording with no source at all, which is why the quote is often assumed to be one of the Hepburn fakes. It is not.
source.excerptNote: Printed as direct speech, in answer to a question about why audiences felt such empathy for her. The passage continues; the circulating version of the line drops “myself” and adds a comma.

author.name: Audrey Hepburn
author.heading: Who said it
author.metaLine: 1929–1993 · Belgian-born actress and UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador
author.bio: Born in Ixelles, Brussels in 1929 and raised partly in the occupied Netherlands, Hepburn became one of the defining screen presences of the 1950s and ’60s in Roman Holiday, Sabrina, Breakfast at Tiffany’s and My Fair Lady. She stepped away from full-time acting in 1966 to raise her sons, and spent her final years as a Goodwill Ambassador for UNICEF, travelling to famine and war zones on the fund’s behalf. She died at her home in Tolochenaz, Switzerland in January 1993, less than two years after giving the interview this line comes from.

misattribution.heading: The wording, and the company it keeps
misattribution.intro: This one holds up — which is not the way most sentences on an Audrey Hepburn quote page end. The only thing worth correcting is a missing word, and the only thing worth warning about is what sits next to it on aggregator pages.

items.why: The Times printed her words as “I myself was born with an enormous need for affection and a terrible need to give it” — the version that travels drops “myself” and adds a comma. It is a trim, not a rewrite, but the fuller line is the one she actually spoke, per the article itself ↗.

The “Time Tested Beauty Tips” (“For attractive lips, speak words of kindness…”) sold on posters under Hepburn’s name were written by the humorist Sam Levenson in his 1973 book In One Era and Out the Other. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the tips “were spoken by her, but she did not claim credit for them.”

The “I believe in pink… I believe in miracles” passage is filed under Misattributed on Wikiquote ↗, which traces it to an unidentified MySpace member circa 2007–08 and notes no evidence of it during Hepburn’s lifetime.

misattribution.truthLine: The affection line is the real one, and it is datable to the day: she said it to Alan Riding in Switzerland, and The New York Times ran it on 22 April 1991, Section C, Page 13 ↗.

context.heading: Why she said it
lead: The remark was not a piece of inspirational filler — it was Hepburn trying to explain her own appeal, reluctantly. Riding had pressed her on why audiences felt such empathy for her: was it the beauty, the vulnerability, the humour? She hedged first (“It’s impossible for me to know”), said that for her the thing always had to do with “some kind of affection, love, a warmth,” and only then offered the sentence that has outlived the interview.

She was 61, had lived in Switzerland since 1964, had given up her career in 1966 to be home when her children came back from school, and was by then working for UNICEF rather than for studios. The tribute she was being interviewed about frightened her: “absolutely marvelous, but it’s also absolutely terrifying,” she told the paper, adding that she had written her thanks down in case she blanked out.
context.detailsSummary: The childhood the interview keeps returning to
detailsBody: Riding notes that Hepburn kept circling back to her childhood to explain her approach to life. Born in Belgium to a Dutch mother and an English father, she spent her early years in England, then returned to the Netherlands after her parents separated and lived through the Nazi occupation: an uncle and a cousin of her mother’s were shot, a brother was sent to a labour camp in Germany, and by the end of the war the family in Arnhem, without water or electricity, was eating tulip bulbs to stay alive.

What kept her going, she said, was wanting to dance — “My dream was to wear a tutu and dance at Covent Garden.” Placed next to that, the sentence about needing affection reads less like a slogan and more like an account of where the need came from.
context.pull: That’s what I’d like to think maybe has been the appeal.
